Orchot Tzadikim 26:17: Also they are not careful about envy, hatred, slander, pride, anger, and all the traits discussed in this book. Also they are not careful about matters of fulfilling the commandments that depend on action, such as washing the hands, and matters of damages between one person and another, and observing the Sabbath properly.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:18: And many stumble in this, for it is a very simple matter: whoever is not expert in the commandments stumbles in many places. And in this way a person commits transgressions all his days without noticing. So this repentant person must know the transgressions he has committed. And how can a person know this? Let him study the commandments, and understand, for each and every commandment, what is lacking in it that he did not fulfill and in what he transgressed. And if he does not know in what he transgressed, how can he regret it? Rather, he must know the transgression in order to regret it, as the verse says, "for I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me" (Psalms 51:5).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:19: The second: even when he knows the transgressions he committed, he will not regret them if he does not know for certain the evil of the transgressions he committed. For if he thinks: "what does it matter if I enjoyed this world without a blessing, or if I was idle from Torah? This is not so bad a thing!" — whoever thinks this way will not regret it and will not return with a whole heart. Rather, he must think: "there is nothing as bad in the whole world as one who does not concern himself with the command of the exalted King" — how much more so than a king of flesh and blood: how bad a thing it is to transgress His command.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:20: The third: the sinner must know and believe from the depth of his heart that there is reward and punishment through harsh judgments for the transgressions he committed, and if he does not know this he will not concern himself with returning. But once the punishment becomes clear to him, he will return and regret, and seek forgiveness from the praised God, as it is said, "my flesh trembles for fear of You, and I am afraid of Your judgments" (Psalms 119:120).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:21: The fourth: the sinner must know that all the transgressions he committed throughout his life, great and small, and all the bad thoughts and idle words, and all his affairs from small to great — all are written in the book. And there is no forgetting before the exalted Lord, as it is written, "is it not stored up with Me, sealed up in My treasuries?" (Deuteronomy 32:34); and it says, "He seals up the hand of every man" (Job 37:7). For if he thinks there is forgetting regarding his iniquities, he will not regret them and will not seek forgiveness for them. For many think that because the Holy One, blessed be He, delays in exacting payment for transgressions, they will be forgotten and He will not come to judge them for them, as it is said, "because sentence against an evil deed is not executed quickly, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil" (Ecclesiastes 8:11).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:22: The fifth: that he know truly that teshuvah is a complete remedy for transgressions. For a sick person who does not believe that the remedy given him will heal him will not concern himself with eating the remedy or drinking the medicine. But when he knows for certain the benefit of the medicine and the drink, he will desire to bear the bitterness of the remedy. So too, when he knows for certain the benefit of teshuvah, he will desire to attain the levels of teshuvah.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:23: The sixth: he must think in his heart of the good things the Blessed Creator has done for him from his beginning until this day, and he ought to have given thanks for the good things, yet instead he did nothing but transgress His commandments. And he should weigh the punishment of the transgression against its sweetness, and the reward of the commandment against its difficulty in this world, as the Sages said: reckon the loss [incurred by performing] a commandment against its reward, and the reward [gained by performing] a transgression against its loss (Mishnah Avot 2:1).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:24: The seventh: he must know to strengthen himself very much, and to bear great suffering in refraining from the evil he was accustomed to. For this is a very simple matter: a transgression one has been accustomed to all his days seems to him like something permitted (Yoma 86b), and it is very hard for him to separate from it. Therefore a person needs great strengthening and very great fences to separate from what he was accustomed to, and needs a great resolve with all his heart and all his soul to refrain. And he should remove the habit from his heart as though he had never been accustomed to it, and accustom himself to despise the evil in his heart, as it is said, "and rend your heart, and not your garments" (Joel 2:13). And when the sinner fixes these seven matters in his heart, he is then close to the path of teshuvah.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:25: And behold, there are many levels of teshuvah, and according to the levels a person draws near to the exalted Lord. And the soul is never purified with complete purity, so that the iniquities be as though they never were, except after a person purifies his heart. It is like a soiled garment: if you wash it a little, the dirt will pass, but a mark or stain will remain in it; but with much washing it will become entirely white. And so it is written, "wash me thoroughly from my iniquity" (Psalms 51:4). Therefore wash your heart from iniquity, as it is written, "wash your heart from wickedness, O Jerusalem" (Jeremiah 4:14).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:26: And now I must write you twenty matters that are among the foundations of teshuvah:
Orchot Tzadikim 26:27: The first: he should take hold of the trait of regret. And he should take to heart that there is great punishment for whoever transgresses the command of the great King, as the verse says (Jeremiah 13:16), "give glory to the Lord your God, before it grows dark..." And when a person thinks of the days of darkness that will come upon whoever transgresses against the God of Jacob, he will fear greatly and regret his deeds, and say in his heart: "what have I done? How was the fear of God not before my eyes! How did I not dread the reproofs for my iniquity! How did I not rule over my inclination for the pleasure of a single moment! How did I defile my pure soul, which was breathed into me from the source of holiness! How did I exchange a great and long-lasting world, enduring forever, for a small, perishable world! How did I not remember the day of death, when nothing will remain before my soul but my own corpse and dust!" And so he should increase such thoughts in his heart on this matter. And this is the matter Jeremiah spoke of (Jeremiah 8:6), "no man repented of his wickedness, saying, 'what have I done?'"
Orchot Tzadikim 26:28: The second: abandoning the sin — that the sinner abandon his evil ways, and resolve with all his heart that he will not return to that evil path again. And this is the beginning of teshuvah: to abandon his evil ways and thoughts, to agree in his heart and accept upon himself that he will not sin again, and to turn back the evil thought he has thought, and to cut off his evil deeds from his hand.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:29: The third: sorrow — that he sigh in bitterness of heart. For if a person loses a single coin, it is hard for him; and if he loses his wealth, he will mourn and his heart will be bitter within him; and likewise if other troubles befall him, he will grieve greatly. How much more so should one grieve who has rebelled against the great Master and corrupted his way before Him, when He had done him kindness — how much more should he grieve at every moment. And know that the levels and virtues of teshuvah correspond to the greatness of the bitterness and grief over the transgressions committed, for the grief comes from the purity of the supernal soul; and the Holy One, blessed be He, has compassion on a person when his soul is steeped in grief over his transgressions. And the parable for this: a king has more compassion for the members of his own household, who are close to him and are among the honored nobles of the land, than he has compassion for the villagers. Therefore, when the soul that was separated from above, from a holy place, is in grief, the Maker of all will quickly receive it.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:30: The fourth: sorrow and grief expressed in action. Until now we have spoken of grief and sorrow in the heart; this fourth matter is sorrow and grief in action, as it is said (Joel 2:12), "yet even now, says the Lord, return to Me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning." And he must show signs of sorrow and grief in his garments, such as girding himself with sackcloth, as it is said (Jonah 3:8), "but let man and beast be covered with sackcloth." And he should remove his precious garments from himself, and diminish pleasures: in kinds of food and drink and outings. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Yerushalmi Berachot 1:5): the heart and the eyes are the two brokers of sin, and it is written (Numbers 15:39), "and you shall not go about after your own heart and after your own eyes." Therefore the iniquity of these two brokers is atoned for in this way: the iniquity of the heart's brokerage through bitterness and grief, and the iniquity of the eyes' brokerage is atoned for through tears, as it is said (Psalms 119:136), "streams of water run down my eyes, because they do not keep Your Torah" — he did not say "because I did not keep" but "because they do not keep," meaning: these eyes were the spies that sought out the sin, therefore I have let streams of water flow down. And when he weeps over his transgressions and afflicts himself, let him say: "my tears shall extinguish Your burning wrath; and the return of my deeds shall turn Your wrath away from me; and the arrangement of my table, which I have not arranged [as a feast], shall be counted as an arranged altar; and the pot I have not set upon coals shall be as fire burning upon Your altar; and the deficiency of my blood shall atone like blood upon the horns of the altar; and the diminishment of my fat shall be as the fat of the sacrificial portions; and the sound of my weeping shall be as the sound of singers singing; and the smell of my soul's hunger shall be as the smell of incense; and the weakness of my limbs shall be as the pieces of an offering; and the breaking of my heart shall tear up the books in which my iniquities are written; and the change of my precious garments shall be as priestly garments; and my abstention from bathing shall be as the sanctification of hands and feet; and my acts of return shall bring me back to You; for I have repented of the evil deeds I have done, and I will not return to do evil before You."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:31: The fifth: worry — that he worry over the punishment for his iniquities. For there are iniquities for which teshuvah suspends atonement and sufferings cleanse (Yoma 86a), as it is said (Psalms 38:19), "for I will declare my iniquity, I will be sorrowful for my sin." And what is the difference between "sorrow" and "worry"? Sorrow is over what has already passed, while worry is over the future — that he always worry lest he fall short in the matter of teshuvah, and not complete the requirement of teshuvah. And let him worry lest his inclination overpower him, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Mishnah Avot 2:4): do not trust in yourself until the day of your death.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:32: The sixth: shame, as it is said (Jeremiah 31:18), "I am ashamed, yes, even disgraced, for I bear the reproach of my youth." And behold, the sinner is very ashamed to commit a transgression before people — how then should he not be ashamed before the Holy One, blessed be He?! And we have already explained the matter of shame in the Gate of Shame.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:33: The seventh: submission with a whole heart, and lowliness. For whoever recognizes his Maker will know in what he has transgressed against His words, and will humble himself and submit. And it is written (Psalms 51:19), "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" — "a broken spirit" is a lowly spirit. Submission is among the foundations of teshuvah, and through submission a person draws near to the Blessed Lord, as it is said (Isaiah 66:2), "but to this one will I look, to him who is poor and of a contrite spirit." And the highest level of the submission required by the path of teshuvah is that he magnify and glorify the service of the Creator, and not credit himself with good, but regard everything as small in his own eyes compared to what he is obligated to do in the service of the Blessed Lord. Therefore let him submit and serve modestly, and not covet honor for his good deeds.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:34: The eighth: submission in action — that he conduct himself with a gentle answer. If a person reviles him for his former deeds, let him remain silent, or say, "I know that I have sinned." And he should not make fine garments and ornaments for himself, as it is said (Exodus 33:5), "and now, put off your ornaments from yourself." And his eyes should always be downcast, as it is said (Job 22:29), "and He shall save the one of downcast eyes." And the signs of submission are: a gentle answer, a low voice, and downcast eyes. And these matters humble the heart.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:35: The ninth: breaking desire. Let him take to heart that desire corrupts all deeds, and let him abstain from excess even in what is permitted to him, taking only enough to satisfy his soul and sustain his body, and likewise regarding his wife. For as long as a person follows desire, he is drawn after the workings of the body and distances himself from the path of the intellective soul, as it is written (Deuteronomy 32:15), "and Jeshurun grew fat and kicked"; and it is written (Proverbs 30:9), "lest I be full, and deny, and say, who is the Lord?" And behold, the desire placed in a person's heart is the root of all his actions, therefore let him hasten to correct his desire, as we have already elaborated above. And there is great benefit in breaking desire, for by this he reveals that his heart is good and upright, since he despises the very nature that caused him to sin. And whoever abstains even from what is permitted has thereby built a great fence so that he not come near what is forbidden, as if to say: "behold, even in what is permitted I will not fully satisfy my desire — how then shall I stretch out my hand into what is forbidden?!"
Orchot Tzadikim 26:36: The tenth: to restore his deed. How so? Whoever gazed at forbidden women should conduct himself with downcast eyes; whoever engaged in slander should occupy himself with Torah (Arachin 15b). And with every limb with which he sinned, let him strive to fulfill commandments with it. And so our Sages said: with the limb one sins, one makes amends. And our Sages further said (Vayikra Rabbah 21:5): if you have committed bundles of transgressions, perform bundles of commandments against them; feet that hastened to run to transgression should hasten to run to a commandment; a mouth that spoke rebellion should have its palate utter truth, and its mouth should open with wisdom; hands that shed innocent blood should open the hand to the poor; haughty eyes should become crushed and downcast; a heart that devises wicked thoughts should hide within it the sayings of the Torah.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:37: The eleventh: examining his ways, as it is said (Lamentations 3:40), "let us search and examine our ways, and return to the Lord." And the examination is that he inspect himself for the transgressions he committed in his days. And there is benefit in this for three things: the first, that he remember all the matters in which he sinned and confess them all, for confession is among the foundations of atonement. The second, that he know how many transgressions and sins he has, and through this add submission. The third, that even though he accepts upon himself to abandon every sin, he must know the matters in which he sinned, in order to make a fence to be careful of those matters in which he stumbled. For a person needs more guarding regarding those transgressions he was accustomed to, and which are light in his eyes to commit, and over which the inclination rules. And he is like a sick person: when he begins to recover, he must be careful about several matters so that they not return him to his illness; so too whoever is sick from transgressions must be very careful when he begins to return.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:38: The twelfth: that he investigate and know the gravity of each of his iniquities, and in which transgression there is flogging, or death by the court, or excision (karet). And when he knows the gravity of the sin, let him embitter his heart in confession and add submission.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:39: The thirteenth: that light transgressions appear to him as though grave, such as gazing at women and speaking much with them, or idle talk, or going about idle, or mentioning the Name of Heaven in vain — all these and many more like them, which in the eyes of many people, even in the eyes of the great of the generation, are considered light — should be considered by him very grave. And there are four reasons for this: the first, that one should not look at the smallness of the transgression, but at the greatness of the King who warned against it. A parable of a king who commanded two of his servants: he commanded one to bring him drink because he was very thirsty, and he commanded the other to do something not so necessary, and warned each of them upon his own life — certainly whoever transgresses is liable for death, for one is punished for stealing a single coin just as one is punished for stealing a thousand, since each transgresses the king's command. So too, regarding the whole Torah He warned (Deuteronomy 27:1), "keep all the commandment which I command you this day," and it is written (ibid. verse 26), "cursed be he who does not uphold the words of this Torah, to do them." The second: whoever transgresses the light sin many times — it then becomes grave, for the punishments accumulate each and every time. The third: when he is accustomed to transgressions, and they become to him as though permitted, and he does not guard against them — he is counted among those who throw off the yoke and an apostate regarding one thing. The fourth: for it is the way of the inclination that when it triumphs in a light matter, it then triumphs in a grave matter. Therefore the Sages said (Mishnah Avot 2:1): be as careful with a light commandment as with a grave one. And they further said (ibid. 4:2): one commandment leads to another commandment, and one transgression leads to another transgression.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:40: The fourteenth: confession, as it is said (Leviticus 5:5), "and he shall confess that he has sinned in that thing." And he is obligated to mention his own iniquities and the iniquities of his ancestors. And why should he confess the sins of his ancestors? Because he is punished when he holds onto his ancestors' deeds, and so it is written (Leviticus 26:40), "and they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers." And he must be very careful, at the time of confession, to resolve in his heart to abandon his evil ways, for if he returns to them and does not abandon them, he is like one who immerses [in a ritual bath] while holding an impure creeping thing (Ta'anit 16a). For confession is like immersion, and the sin is like the creeping thing, and it is a clear matter that immersion does not help one who still holds the creeping thing.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:41: The fifteenth: prayer — that the sinner pray to the Blessed Lord, and ask the Blessed Lord to help him in his teshuvah, and open for him the gates of purity.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:42: The sixteenth: correcting the wrong — that he correct everything he has done wrong. For instance, if he robbed a person, he should return the stolen item before confession, so that his confession be accepted. And if he robbed a person and has nothing with which to repay, let him pray to God that He grant him the means to repay.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:43: The seventeenth: pursuing deeds of kindness and truth, as it is said (Proverbs 16:6), "by kindness and truth iniquity is atoned for." And if the sinner has not returned to the Blessed Lord, his iniquity will not be atoned for by his deed of kindness, as the verse says (Deuteronomy 10:17), "who regards not persons, nor takes reward." And the Sages explained: "nor takes reward" — to forgive the commandments and overlook the iniquities. And this verse, "by kindness and truth iniquity is atoned for," speaks of those who do teshuvah, for there are transgressions for which teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend atonement, and sufferings cleanse. And behold, kindness shields the sinner and guards him from suffering, and also saves him from death, as it is said (Proverbs 10:2), "but righteousness delivers from death." And there is further the iniquity of desecrating the Name, for which teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend atonement and death cleanses, as it is said (Isaiah 22:14), "surely this iniquity shall not be atoned for you until you die." And when a person strives to hold fast to truth in his hand, and strengthens the hands of men of truth and lifts up their heads, and humbles men of falsehood and brings them down to the dust — behold, these are the ways of sanctifying the Name. And when a person is stirred by the trait of truth, then the iniquity of desecration will be forgiven him along with his teshuvah.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:44: The eighteenth: that his sins be always before him, and that he not forget them, as it is written (Psalms 51:5), "for I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:45: The nineteenth: abandoning the sin when it comes into his hand while he is in the full strength of his desire. And the Sages said (Yoma 86b): who is the repentant sinner whose teshuvah reaches the Throne of Glory? This is one who has been tested and comes out clean, at the same period, in the same place, and with the same woman. Its meaning: when the sin comes his way while he is in the strength of his inclination, and he subdues his inclination out of fear of the Blessed Lord. And if this circumstance does not come his way, let him increase the fear of the Blessed Lord in his soul day by day. Let him do this all his days, and this is a supreme level of teshuvah.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:46: The twentieth: to bring back many from iniquity, as far as is in his power, as it is said (Ezekiel 18:30), "return, and turn back from all your transgressions" — we learn from this that this is among the foundations of teshuvah. And it is said (Leviticus 19:17), "you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him" — we learn from this that if he does not rebuke him, he will be punished for his sins. And so David said (Psalms 51:15), "I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners shall return to You."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:47: Twenty-four things hold back teshuvah. Four of them are a great iniquity, and whoever does one of these four — the Holy One, blessed be He, does not enable him to do teshuvah in proportion to the greatness of his sin. And these are: causing the many to sin, and included in this iniquity is one who prevents the many from performing a commandment. And one who leads the many or his fellow astray from a good path to a bad path, such as an inciter or a seducer. And one who sees his son take up a wicked way of life and does not restrain him, for had he restrained him he would have separated, so it follows that he causes him to sin. And included in this iniquity is anyone who has the power to protest against others, whether many or individuals, and does not protest, but leaves them to their own stumbling. And one who says, "I will sin and repent." And included in this: one who says, "I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone," for whoever thinks this way finds it very hard to do teshuvah, for he will always sin, since he thinks he will repent, and so the transgression is light in his eyes.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:48: Of those twenty-four things, five of them lock the paths of teshuvah before those who commit them. And these are: one who separates himself from the community when they do teshuvah, and says, "peace be upon my own soul," and does not grieve in the community's grief — therefore he does not merit in the merit they gain. And one who disputes the words of the Sages, since dispute causes him to separate from them, and he does not know the paths of teshuvah. And one who mocks the commandments, for since they have become disgraceful in his eyes, he does not concern himself with performing them — and if he does not perform them, by what will he merit? And one who demeans his teachers, for this matter causes him to be driven off and banished from the world like that man [Elisha ben Avuyah], and at the time he is banished he will not find a teacher to show him the way of truth. And one who hates rebukes, for he has thereby left himself no path of teshuvah, since rebukes bring about teshuvah. For when a person is made aware of his sins and shamed, he returns in teshuvah, as it is said (Deuteronomy 9:7), "remember, do not forget... you were rebellious against the Lord"; "yet the Lord has not given you a heart to know..." (ibid. 29:3); "a foolish nation and unwise..." (ibid. 32:6). And so Isaiah the prophet rebuked Israel until they returned in teshuvah. Therefore every community must appoint one of their sages, an elder who has feared Heaven from his youth and is beloved by them, to rebuke the community and bring them back in teshuvah. And whoever hates rebukes does not come to the one who rebukes and does not listen to his words, and therefore remains in his sins, which are good in his own eyes.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:49: Of those twenty-four things there are five, such that whoever does them cannot do complete teshuvah, since they are transgressions between a person and his fellow, and he does not know that his fellow was wronged by him, so as to ask his forgiveness. And these are: one who curses the multitude, and did not curse a known individual so that he could ask his forgiveness. And one who shares in the gain of a thief, for he thinks this is not theft since "I did not steal"; and even if he wishes to return and repent, to whom shall he return it? For he does not know from whom the thief stole, and he strengthens the thief's hand and causes him to sin further. And one who finds a lost object and does not announce it in order to return it to its owner, so that when he wishes to do teshuvah, he does not know whose it was. And one who devours the property of the poor, orphans, and widows: these are wretched people, unknown and unrecognized, wandering from city to city, and this one who devours their property does not know whose it is to return it. And some say the word is related to "pressure," meaning: he presses these poor people over a debt they owe him until he takes their lands or movable property in settlement for less than their worth, and he does not think there is any sin in this, for he says, "I am only taking what is mine!" And one who accepts a bribe to bend justice, and does not know how far this bending reaches and how great its effect is, so as to make the matter right. And further: he strengthens the hand of the one for whom he bent the judgment and causes him to sin.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:50: Of those twenty-four things there are five, such that whoever does them is not presumed to repent of them, since they are light matters in the eyes of most people, so that a person sins and it does not seem to him like a sin. And these are: one who eats from a meal that is not sufficient for its host. For instance, a person who enters a poor man's house, and the poor man invites him to eat much, but does not do so willingly, only because he is ashamed before him to offer little — and this guest does not consider it a sin, for he thinks he eats with the host's permission and not against his will. And one who makes use of a poor man's pledge, even if it is only an axe or a plow, and says in his heart, "I have not caused them any lack, and I have not robbed them." And one who gazes at forbidden women, for the one gazing thinks in his heart, "there is nothing to this" — for he says, "did I have relations, or did I draw near?!" And he does not know that the sight of the eye is a great iniquity that leads to the actual act of forbidden relations, as it is said (Numbers 15:39), "and you shall not go about after your own heart and after your own eyes." And one who glorifies himself through his fellow's disgrace says in his heart that he has not sinned, since his fellow is not standing there with him, and no shame has come to him and he has not shamed him — rather, he merely presents his own good deeds and his wisdom and sharpness as greater than his fellow's deeds, wisdom, and sharpness, and the listener will hold him in honor and his fellow in contempt. And one who suspects worthy people in his heart, and says he has not sinned, for he says: "what have I done? I have not done anything, only suspected in general!" And he does not know that suspicion is a great iniquity, for it makes a worthy person seem, in his mind, like a habitual sinner.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:51: Of those twenty-four things there are five, such that whoever does them is continually drawn after them, and it is hard to separate from them. Therefore a person must be very careful about them lest he cling to them, and they are all very bad. And these are: talebearing; slander; a man of anger; a man of evil thoughts; and one who associates with a wicked person, because he learns from his deeds. For when he is always with the wicked man and sees his deeds, they become imprinted in his heart. And this is what Solomon said: "but the companion of fools shall be broken" (Proverbs 13:20).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:52: All these matters and the like of them, even though they hold back teshuvah, nonetheless do not prevent teshuvah. Rather, if a person does teshuvah for them, he is indeed a repentant sinner, and has a share in the World to Come.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:53: Iniquities are of two kinds: one is between a person and the Omnipresent alone, such as tefillin, tzitzit, and sukkah, and the like of these. The second kind is between a person and his fellow. Regarding those transgressions between a person and the Omnipresent, he should do teshuvah in that same matter he transgressed. For instance: if he did not fulfill a positive commandment, let him strive to fulfill it; if he did not occupy himself with acts of kindness, let him toil from the time of his teshuvah onward to do kindness; and if he transgressed a negative commandment, let him resolve in his heart not to transgress it from now on.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:54: In sum: whoever wishes to be among the complete repentant sinners must wage a great war within his heart. And the matter is not as people think, that only those who have committed known transgressions are considered repentant sinners, such as one who had relations with a Samaritan woman or a married woman, or who stole, or the like of these. But this is not so, for there are many robbers who do not know they are robbers, such as one who summons his fellow to judgment, knowing he owes him nothing at all, but intending to provoke him, grieve him, and cause him loss so that he squander his money — and he does not consider in his heart that this matter is robbery. A person who administers an oath to his fellow, even in a lawful case, has a punishment for this. And along these lines a person commits bundles of transgressions every day and every hour. How so? A person is obligated to pray with intent and recite all blessings with intent, and there are few in the world who direct their intent with all their heart. And so in all the commandments there are matters that even the great of this generation are not careful about, because they do not take them to heart and because they do not study the commandments and the good traits. Therefore whoever's heart moves him to do complete teshuvah should be accustomed to studying this book of traits, and in it he will see his error in what he has erred all his days, and reflect on every single matter he reads, whether he has fulfilled it or not. And if he sees that he has not fulfilled it, let him strive and exert himself with all his strength to fulfill it. And he should also be accustomed to the book of the commandments, studying it and understanding each commandment according to its law, and take to heart, for every commandment, to fulfill it as it is stated. And this matter is the great path in the ways of teshuvah — to do teshuvah for each and every matter individually.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:55: There are transgressions between a person and his fellow that are very hard to correct and to do teshuvah for. For instance, a person accustomed to robbery all his days, who does not know from whom he robbed, or does not know where he lives, or perhaps he has gone overseas, or perhaps he lost the money and has nothing to return. And there is one who has been accustomed to transgressions all his days until he is habituated and practiced in them, as it is said (Jeremiah 9:4), "they have taught their tongue to speak falsehood, they weary themselves to commit iniquity."
Orchot Tzadikim 26:56: And there is one who had relations with a forbidden woman and fathered a son from her, and the disgrace will never depart. And there is one accustomed to false words and to relating the disgrace of people. And there is one who led people astray, misleading them into a forbidden matter. And there is one who sees people walking a bad path and straying from the straight way, and this person was afraid of them to rebuke them, or was ashamed before them, until he refrained from showing them the straight way; of him the verse says (Ezekiel 3:18), "he shall die in his iniquity, but his blood will I require at your hand."
